source.version: Published proceedings paper, Proceedings of the 59th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences, 2026, printed pp. 95-103 (PDF pp. 1-9; proceedings identification on PDF p. 1).
source.title_on_document: The Confidence Cage: How Creative Self-Efficacy Hinders Gen AI-Augmented Ideation

supplement.holds: No supplementary material or online appendix is mentioned. The complete PDF contains the main paper and references, ending on PDF p. 9 (printed p. 103); there is no appendix. All reported results are in the main paper, including Tables 1-3 and Figures 1-2 on PDF pp. 5-7 (printed pp. 99-101).

paper_design_summary: Prolific adults completed a baseline fork Alternative Uses Test and were then randomly assigned to a custom GPT-4o coach or a text-only web-search tool for a Frisbee Alternative Uses Test in the same online session (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1-3.2). The final analyzed sample was 300 people, 150 per arm, and the assigned tools were available during the scored post-test (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1-3.2; p. 6, Table 2). An automated language-model system scored the generated uses for composite creativity; ideation and baseline creative self-efficacy were self-reports used in mediation and moderation analyses (PDF pp. 4-5, Section 3.3; pp. 6-7, Table 3).

studies.label: Online pre-test/post-test experiment: GPT-4o coaching versus web search

assignment.what_was_assigned: After the baseline fork task, participants were randomly assigned to Human-AI or Human-Search for the Frisbee post-test. Condition was between participants and time (pre-test versus post-test) was within participants, described as a 2 × 2 mixed factorial design (PDF p. 4 [printed p. 98], Sections 3.1-3.2).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions for the post-test task with control.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 98), Sections 3.1 Design and participants and 3.2 Procedure.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement or registration link is given in the full PDF; methods are on PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.1-3.4.

arms.name: Human-AI
arms.description: Custom GPT-4o chatbot available during the post-test, asking probing questions and offering perspectives without direct task solutions. Copy-paste was disabled; participants were instructed to use it as a collaborative thinking tool (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2). The arm count is the final analyzed count (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Table 2).

arms.name: Human-Search
arms.description: Custom text-only web search engine available during the post-test, intended for inspiration; visual stimuli were eliminated and the same copy-paste restriction applied (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2). The arm count is the final analyzed count (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Table 2).

participants.exclusions: 327 people were recruited, and 27 were excluded from analyses: verbatim copying of complete internet responses (n = 15), failure to follow instructions (n = 8), incomplete task completion (n = 3), and chatbot system error (n = 1). The final analyzed sample was 300 people, with 150 analyzed per arm. The paper does not separately give the number randomized before exclusions or exclusions by arm; recruited and final analyzed counts are not coded as randomized counts (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1).
participants.who: Adults recruited through Prolific; eligibility required age at least 18, English fluency, and residence in the United States or Canada (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1).
participants.country: United States or Canada (residence eligibility; country-specific analyzed counts not stated)
participants.quote: The final sample included 300 participants, with 150 assigned to each experimental condition.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 98), Section 3.1 Design and participants; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 100), Table 2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 101), Table 3 note (N = 300).

ai_tool.name_model: Custom chatbot powered by OpenAI's GPT-4o API (PDF p. 4 [printed p. 98], Section 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: During the Frisbee AUT, the chatbot asked probing questions and offered new perspectives to stimulate divergent thinking, without providing direct solutions. Copy-paste was disabled and participants were instructed to treat it as a collaborative thinking tool. The intervention model is identified, but an exact dated model snapshot and the system prompt are not provided (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2).

task.description: Guilford Alternative Uses Test: generate as many creative and unusual uses as possible for a fork at baseline and a Frisbee at post-test, emphasizing novelty and practicality. The baseline task preceded assignment, and the assigned aid was used during the post-test (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.2-3.3).
task.duration: 5 minutes for each AUT task; approximately 25-30 minutes for the online session (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2).

outcomes.name: Post-test composite creativity score on Frisbee alternative uses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: An LLM-based automated system, citing Organisciak et al. (2023), evaluated novelty, usefulness, and divergence from typical applications and produced a composite creativity score (PDF p. 4 [printed p. 98], Section 3.3, continuing on p. 5 [printed p. 99]). Separate component scores, the exact scoring model/version, score scale, and aggregation of multiple responses into each participant score are not specified. The reported analysis is at participant level. Creativity is the H1 endpoint, but no explicit primary-outcome designation or preregistration is stated (PDF p. 3 [printed p. 97], H1; p. 5 [printed p. 99], Sections 3.4 and 4). Unadjusted and baseline-adjusted comparisons, pre/post displays, and mediation/moderation analyses concern this same outcome (PDF pp. 5-7 [printed pp. 99-101], Tables 1-3 and Figure 1). The methods specify 5,000 bootstrap samples and 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals for mediation (PDF p. 5 [printed p. 99], Section 3.4). Indirect effects through self-reported ideation and condition-by-CSE coefficients are ancillary analyses, not additional observed creativity outcomes or subgroup total treatment effects. The scored post-test was produced with the assigned tool available (PDF p. 4 [printed p. 98], Section 3.2).

contrasts.reported: Unadjusted post-test, Table 2 (analyzed participants): Human-AI n = 150, M = 3.21, SD = 0.22; Human-Search n = 150, M = 2.98, SD = 0.31. Baseline values in the same table: Human-AI M = 2.94, SD = 0.37; Human-Search M = 2.85, SD = 0.38 (PDF p. 6, Table 2). ANCOVA controlling for baseline creativity, age, work experience, gender, and race: F(1, 293) = 58.28, p < .001, η²p = .166. The results prose gives adjusted Human-AI M = 3.19, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [3.15, 3.24], versus Human-Search M = 2.99, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [2.95, 3.04]; adjusted mean difference = 0.20 points and Cohen's d = 0.77. R² = .251, adjusted R² = .235 (PDF p. 5, Section 4). UNRESOLVED SOURCE CONFLICT (flagged by both screeners): Table 2 instead prints adjusted Human-Search M = 3.19 [3.15, 3.24] and Human-AI M = 2.99 [2.95, 3.04], reversing the arm labels relative to the results prose. Both versions are retained as printed; no definitive adjusted arm labels are selected. The coded direction follows the unadjusted values, results prose, and Figure 1, not the contradictory adjusted column (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 4, Table 2 and Figure 1). Path analysis: direct condition effect on creativity after accounting for ideation B = 0.169, SE = 0.032, z = 5.25, p < .001; Table 3 gives 95% CI [0.110, 0.232]. Ideation-to-creativity path B = 0.030, SE = 0.012, z = 2.50, p = .013; Table 3 gives 95% CI [0.009, 0.055]. Creativity-model R² = .298. Table 3 also reports Condition × MOD for the creativity outcome: B = 0.051**, SE = 0.016, 95% CI [0.004, 0.104], where ** denotes p < .01 (PDF p. 6, Section 4 and Table 3; p. 7, Table 3 note). Indirect condition effect on creativity through self-reported ideation: B = 0.031, SE = 0.013, z = 2.38, p = .017, 95% CI [0.010, 0.062]. Conditional indirect effects: low CSE (−1 SD), B = 0.040, SE = 0.017, z = 2.40, p = .016, 95% CI [0.013, 0.080]; mean CSE, B = 0.031, SE = 0.013, z = 2.38, p = .017, 95% CI [0.010, 0.062]; high CSE (+1 SD), B = 0.021, SE = 0.010, z = 2.18, p = .029, 95% CI [0.006, 0.050]. Index of moderated mediation B = −0.008, SE = 0.004, z = −2.05, p = .040; Table 3 gives 95% CI [−0.021, −0.001]. High-minus-low difference B = −0.019, SE = 0.009, z = −2.05, p = .041; Table 3 gives 95% CI [−0.048, −0.003] (PDF p. 6, Section 4 and Table 3). The methods specify 5,000 bootstrap samples and 95% bias-corrected intervals for mediation (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4). The standardizer for the reported Cohen's d is not stated (PDF p. 5, Sections 3.4 and 4). Direct, indirect, and interaction estimates are ancillary results for the same creativity outcome, distinct from the main ANCOVA total contrast.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 98), Section 3.1: analyzed participant counts; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 99), Section 3.4: bootstrap method, and Section 4: ANCOVA statistics; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 100), Table 2: unadjusted arm statistics and contradictory adjusted labels, Figure 1: direction, Section 4 and Table 3: path and indirect-effect statistics; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 101), Table 3 note: condition coding and significance symbols.

eligibility.reason: Final source check confirms all three criteria for S1: participants were randomly assigned to a GPT-4o coach or active text-only web search for the Frisbee Alternative Uses Test (PDF p. 4 [printed p. 98], Sections 3.1-3.2); 300 people were analyzed after exclusions, with 150 analyzed per arm (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6 [printed p. 100], Table 2; p. 7 [printed p. 101], Table 3 note); and their generated uses were scored by an LLM-based automated system for composite creativity (PDF pp. 4-5 [printed pp. 98-99], Section 3.3). Assistance was available during production, supporting with_ai and ai_vs_active (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2). The conflicting adjusted arm labels, unknown initial randomized counts and arm-specific exclusions, unspecified scoring implementation, and unspecified Cohen's d standardizer affect extraction or replication, not these eligibility criteria.

one_line_finding: Among 300 analyzed participants, GPT-4o coaching increased automated AUT creativity versus web search (unadjusted M = 3.21 versus 2.98; reported d = 0.77), but adjusted arm labels conflict between the results prose and Table 2 (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 5, Section 4; p. 6, Table 2).
open_questions: Shared unresolved source conflict: which adjusted arm labels are correct? Section 4 assigns 3.19 [3.15, 3.24] to Human-AI and 2.99 [2.95, 3.04] to Human-Search, whereas Table 2 assigns them to the opposite arms (PDF p. 5 [printed p. 99], Section 4; p. 6 [printed p. 100], Table 2). Figure 1 agrees with the narrative direction but does not settle the contradictory labels; a correction, underlying adjusted-results output, or author clarification is missing.

What were the total and arm-specific randomized counts before exclusions, and exclusions by arm? Section 3.1 gives 327 recruited and 300 analyzed people but no separate initial assignment counts (PDF p. 4 [printed p. 98]); randomized-count fields remain null.

Which exact scoring model/version, score scale, and response-aggregation rule produced the participant creativity composite? These details are not stated in Section 3.3 (PDF pp. 4-5 [printed pp. 98-99]).
Which standard deviation was used for Cohen's d = 0.77? The paper reports the value without specifying its standardizer (PDF p. 5 [printed p. 99], Sections 3.4 and 4).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from both successfully parsed raw forms. Read the entire markdown conversion (all 323 lines, through the references) and extracted text from all nine PDF pages. Inspected the PDF-embedded images for Tables 1-2 and Figures 1-2 in memory, and recovered Table 3 using PyMuPDF find_tables(). The PDF has no appendix. All recorded numerical results were checked against PDF text, recovered table cells, or the embedded table image. PDF locators are one-based; printed proceedings pages are included. No effects, standard errors, or other statistical estimates were calculated. The seven substantive screener differences are additions in B to the reported-statistics field; all are source-supported and retained. A null in a reconciliation a/b value denotes omission from that raw form, not an assertion that the paper lacks the statistic. The same mean-CSE indirect-effect z and p reported explicitly in B already occur in A for the indirect effect with identical B/SE/CI, so that repetition is not counted as a new substantive difference. The forms agree substantively on design, assignment, arms and counts, tool and role, task, outcome inventory and all outcome codes, supplement, sample overlap, company involvement, every eligibility criterion, and finding direction. Wording, added locators, equivalent country-eligibility phrasing, different emphasis in the one-line finding, and empty synthesis placeholder formatting are not substantive differences. The synthesis fields retain the spec defaults because this is an experiment. reconciliation.n_unresolved counts unresolved screener differences only and is zero. This does not settle shared source limitations: both forms already flag the adjusted-arm-label conflict, unknown randomized counts, unspecified scoring implementation, and unspecified Cohen's d standardizer; these remain in open_questions. The shared adjusted-mean conflict is independently confirmed in agreed_fields_checked and both printed versions are preserved in reported; it is not counted as an A-versus-B difference. Only the composite creativity outcome is eligible. Self-reported ideation and baseline CSE are not output scores. Novelty, usefulness, and divergence are components without separate reported outcome estimates. Baseline fork scores are covariates/descriptive measurements within the same outcome. No across-person diversity outcome, AI-withdrawal assessment, later session, additional eligible output outcome, preregistration, or data/code availability URL is reported in the saved document. Participant-level n_units is null because counts are stored as people in participants and arms. open_items.item: Shared unresolved source conflict: which adjusted arm labels are correct? Section 4 assigns 3.19 [3.15, 3.24] to Human-AI and 2.99 [2.95, 3.04] to Human-Search, whereas Table 2 assigns them to the opposite arms (PDF p. 5 [printed p. 99], Section 4; p. 6 [printed p. 100], Table 2). Figure 1 agrees with the narrative direction but does not settle the contradictory labels; a correction, underlying adjusted-results output, or author clarification is missing. This affects extraction of adjusted estimates, not any eligibility criterion. Author confirmation of the corrected arm labels and the underlying adjusted-results output would settle it.

What were the total and arm-specific randomized counts before exclusions, and exclusions by arm? Section 3.1 gives 327 recruited and 300 analyzed people but no separate initial assignment counts (PDF p. 4 [printed p. 98]); randomized-count fields remain null. This affects participant-flow documentation, not eligibility: random assignment is explicit and 300 analyzed people exceed the threshold. Author counts at assignment and a breakdown of exclusions by arm would settle it.

Which exact scoring model/version, score scale, and response-aggregation rule produced the participant creativity composite? These details are not stated in Section 3.3 (PDF pp. 4-5 [printed pp. 98-99]). This affects scoring replication and aggregation details, not criterion 3: the methods explicitly say that generated responses received a composite creativity score. Author scoring documentation, including the model/version, scale, and aggregation rule, would settle it.

Which standard deviation was used for Cohen's d = 0.77? The paper reports the value without specifying its standardizer (PDF p. 5 [printed p. 99], Sections 3.4 and 4). This affects interpretation and later use of the standardized effect, not any eligibility criterion. The authors' exact effect-size formula and standard deviation would settle it.
